paras.t: Introduction

We are used to understanding technology as our extra-organic development, as something external, but in reality it is part of us. The hand-brain relationship has enhanced our knowledge, made us who we are. The tools we have endowed ourselves with (such as, for example, mathematics) are therefore additional organs, and thus an integral part of the evolution of our species (in the essay The Gesture and the Word, Leroi-Gourhan engages in a veritable biology of technique). Marx in the Economic-Philosophical Manuscripts of 1844, describing the becoming of man-industry, states that industry is the true anthropology.

Industrial-technological society is not something negative in itself, as the anarcho-primitivists claim, but a particular evolutionary stage of humanity, which has not been fully understood by humanity, and therefore produces alienation. Capitalism is the prehistory of humanity, but it develops the foundations of future society. As the hand develops the brain, so the computer develops the brain, merging more and more with it. A set of computers combined with a set of brains produces a bio-technological social brain, and this produces effects in society, ranging from fear to amazement.

Technological development will bring about a paradigm shift, it is already doing so. These statements are not to be confused with the ‘techno-solutionism’ that is all the rage in some Silicon Valley circles, a new religion that has replaced God with artificial intelligence. Think of the statements by Eric Schmidt, former CEO of Google, speaking at the AI+ Energy 2024 summit in Washington, where he urged greater development of artificial intelligence, despite the fact that data centres (which provide the necessary computing power) require more and more energy, threatening carbon reduction targets. No worries, says Schmidt, in the absence of global coordination it will be artificial intelligence that will solve the problem of the energy needed for its development. It will also help save the world from climate change. We have some doubts about this, being of the opinion that in this mode of production – machines starve the world (‘Never the commodity will feed man’, 1953-1954).

They are, however, as we shall see, a picklock to blow up existing social relations. Our research on ‘essays on future organisation’ is aimed at detecting and highlighting signs of change within the present mode of production.

In the course of our ‘patrolling’ work on the Net in search of material on the ‘borderlands’ between comatose capitalism and future society, among the many videos on new technologies on YouTube, one in particular caught our attention: it was a round table discussion between editors and contributors of the magazine Limes, entitled ‘Intelligence is not artificial’[[1]], which brings us back to the themes we addressed in the article ‘A system that engineers itself’[[2]], in which we wrote:

“Above the bourgeoisie, therefore the circuits of capital that with their owners act on the surface of the Globe, there can be nothing but a hypothetical circuit in Space. It sounds like a joke, but the warnings show that the path has already begun. And not just now: for market expansion there are always three caravels and a port from which to launch them. In any case, now a good deal of capital already has its instruments in space, where thousands of artificial satellites for all kinds of services rotate on orbits of all sizes. And investments in this field continue in spite of a crisis that has brought the world economy to its knees.”
For some time now, in fact, capital has been investing massively in space. Not only states but also private individuals, such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, are launching satellites into orbit.

In the video, the editor of Limes, Lucio Caracciolo, after a brief presentation, gives the floor to the guests, including the CEO of Leonardo[[3]], Alessandro Profumo, who explains what a ‘digital twin’ is: with a system of space satellites and ground-based sensors, actuators and communication protocols, data processing, self-learning, etc., one can create a ‘digital twin’ of everything, a cybernetic copy of any object, whether civil or military.

We are not fascinated by the presentation the bourgeoisie make of ‘their’ technologies, on which they place great hopes for the salvation of a capitalism with the water at its throat, but neither are we indifferent to them: in fact we know, from Marx’s Capital onwards, that technological development does not save the current mode of production from its contradictions, if anything it is one of the elements that will sink it. The technological infrastructure that makes the new business models possible is, at the same time, the basis of a different social organisation.

With the shift to the massive extraction of relative surplus value (intensification of exploitation by machines), the foundations of capitalism are negated, as already highlighted in Marx’s Grundrisse:

“To the degree that labour time — the mere quantity of labour — is posited by capital as the sole determinant element, to that degree does direct labour and its quantity disappear as the determinant principle of production — of the creation of use values — and is reduced both quantitatively, to a smaller proportion, and qualitatively, as an, of course, indispensable but subordinate moment, compared to general scientific labour, technological application of natural sciences, on one side, and to the general productive force arising from social combination [Gliederung] in total production on the other side — a combination which appears as a natural fruit of social labour (although it is a historic product). Capital thus works towards its own dissolution as the form dominating production.”

Today’s society uses the important achievements of science for narrow purposes, for the accumulation of more capital, for the private appropriation of socially produced value, heedless of the consequences of such actions, which are ever-increasing crises, devastating wars and various types of social catastrophes. But science is not the problem, it is part of the solution.

Human knowledge, as long as it remains within the petty limits of the present social form, is not really knowledge. Although there are numerous models available to Leonardo for the simulation of physical and biological phenomena, none of them is capable of functioning as a model that organises society as a whole. This is the central problem of capitalism: the impossibility of extending the production plan within the factory to the whole of society.

The limitation of bourgeois society is the one highlighted by Engels, namely the waste inherent in a world that is divided into groups and subgroups (‘Capital and the Theory of Waste’, n+1, no. 41). Capitalism is increasingly light and dematerialised, but on the other hand it needs an enormous amount of energy to keep going. If, for example, we were to move from dwellings designed for the ‘autonomous’ family unit, which then means ‘isolated’, to forms of integral cohousing with shared services and spaces, there would immediately be considerable energy savings. The ‘Italian’ Communist Left has produced important material on the issue of capitalist dissipation[[4]], now an issue on the agenda of the summits of the world bourgeoise itself. Think of the unemployment industry, which thrives on increasing the number of people without a job: employment agencies, training courses, bilateral bodies, employment offices, etc. Not to mention the huge waste of social energy caused by the spread of wars: the species dissipates more and more energy to keep up an anti-human system.

The International Monetary Fund has sounded the alarm about electricity consumption due to the crypto and AI industry and the increase in data centre power demand. There is also the problem of water consumption. For example, in the state of Virginia, tech giants such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft consumed something like 7 billion litres of water in 2023 to prevent their servers from overheating, and this figure is set to rise.

Clearly, in order to arrive at a different kind of social organisation, one that is oriented towards the needs of the species and not those of capital, there must be a paradigm shift, which has not yet imposed itself at a general level, but which is making its way through the folds of capitalism, and which we will discuss in the course of this paper.
Lessons from the present

Since we are accustomed to proceeding in our work by chained arguments, as the current we refer to has taught us, it is natural to make connections with previous seminars. In 2016, we gave a couple of lectures on the subject of ‘Lessons of the Future’, taking our cue from a series of notebooks published by Sole 24 Ore, from which a review came out in the journal that we entitled ‘Lessons of the Present’ (n+1, no. 39).

On closer inspection, these were lessons based on today because the technologies under consideration were not technologies of tomorrow but technologies that already existed and were widely used in factories, offices and universities.
It is important for communists not to confuse the present with the future or, even worse, with the past.

We, let us repeat, study the development of these technologies in relation to the development-death dynamic of capitalism (they are mines that will blow up the present society) but, above all, to understand how they can be used in future society, what advantages they can represent for a humanity emancipated from capitalism. They give us an idea of how pregnant this social form is with the future one. The list of technologies that are transforming our society is a long one, ranging from Blockchain, a decentralised and disintermediated system for peer-to-peer exchange, to the Internet of Things, i.e. the connection of objects through the Net. Tools that have the particularity of connecting objects and human beings, forging links between things that were previously separate, overcoming national barriers.
Amadeo used to say that every time a barrier falls, the revolution advances.

To understand the origin of the technologies we are talking about, we need to take a step back, to grasp the historical dynamic on the thread of time. To understand today, and especially tomorrow, one must have knowledge of what happened yesterday. It is therefore essential to understand how we arrived at the immense amount of data produced by industry that is now completely socialised (we are all potentially partial workers in a single global production plan), and that makes it possible for the data’s to function.

The technologies we are dealing with in this paper, including the ‘digital twin’, would not be possible without the Net and without an immense production and recording of bits, generated by an increasingly connected and interactive humanity. As we shall see, big data define the new ‘development’ (perhaps it would be better to say transition) horizon of capitalism. Given the centrality they have assumed in today’s society, economists claim that there is now a data value chain.

Let us remember, however, that the history of data is at one with the history of man, who since ancient times has needed to count and keep track of mathematical operations, which he performed on different types of media.
Communism (already) achievable

Communism, as a reality on the march and not as an ideology, is so mature that even the capitalists realise that significant socio-economic changes must be made – otherwise the current mode of production will be derailed.
These changes can only – if they are indeed such – be anticipations of the future social form.

A few ‘giga capitalists’ (Elon Musk, Sam Altman, etc.) are sounding the alarm about the growth of ‘technological unemployment’, proposing the provision of a universal basic income decoupled from work. Presidents are also making similar proposals: in October 2023, at the Democracy Forum, Barack Obama, discussing the impact of automation, proposed a short working week and a universal basic income. Change is knocking at the door and everyone, from politicians to the Pope, realises that many updates need to be made to the political agenda of the states, the problem is that no representative of Capital is able to tackle the problem at its root being bound by a thousand constraints to bourgeois interests[[5]].

‘Capitalism without capital is today characterised by a strong redistribution of production and income and, as Haskel and Westlake write, by an increase in inequality between and within countries. As noted by the OECD in a 2016 study (Automation and Independent Work in a Digital Economy. Policy Brief on the Future of Work), the new capitalism induces significant short-term unemployment due to the replacement of old jobs and the delay in the transition to new professions. The process of algorithmic data acquisition and processing is, in fact, also extending to the world of professions. According to the Center for Strategy and Competitiveness in Stockholm, many of the functions that are now performed by humans will soon be automated. And we are not just talking about routine, manual tasks, but also non-routine cognitive activities.' (Delmastro, Nicita, Big data. How it is changing our world)

In the academic sphere, some are trying to understand the nature of change and propose solutions: this is the case with the philosopher Maurizio Ferraris (see our review of the essay Documanity. Philosophy of the New World in issue no. 50 of this journal) in some of his counter-current statements, such as that ‘we are closer to realised communism than the resigned believe’, and that ‘communism is a reality already present in our world’.

The philosopher is a bit confused, he thinks of China as a socialist country, but the statements we have quoted are – for all intents and purposes – ideological capitulations in the face of Marxism, an echo of things that the Communist Left and n+1 have been saying for some time, namely as a part of our discussion on how the future society acts on the present one.

For Ferraris, also a supporter of basic income, the Web is the largest recording apparatus that humanity has developed so far: there has never been a time in history when so much data has been recorded as today, and this will lead to substantial changes in the material structure of society. There are some 23 billion connected devices in the world, but there are only 8 billion human beings. These devices produce billions of connections every day, more data than that which is produced in terms of ‘regular’ units of sold manufactured goods by all the factories in the world. An immense amount of transactions and coded traces amounting to 2.5 quintillion bytes.

These are numbers that are linked together by means of algorithms and from which patterns and thus new information is obtained. The ‘new’ capital for Ferraris is no longer something material but is information (which for us is practically synonymous with anti-entropy) and the ability to process it.
We are always connected

If we want to find a symbolic date in which our relationship with the Net and also with the world changes, it is the presentation, on 9 January 2007, of Apple’s first smartphone. Steve Jobs showed the iPhone to the public and described it as the fusion of three devices: iPod with a touch screen, a mobile phone, and the Internet. Within a short time, it was realised that the smartphone was no longer a simple means of communication but a means of production (think of the riders who deliver food or packages to your door: they take their orders from an app). 9 January therefore marks the beginning of a revolution, prepared for by the advent of the first personal computer. The smartphone revolution began, and other big companies would soon start mass-producing them.

Within a few years, everyone will own one. It will soon become part of ourselves, part of our daily lives, and we will not be able to do without it. Before the advent of the smartphone there were two clearly separated worlds: if you had to connect to the Internet you had to be at home, or at an Internet Point, or in some computer room. There was a clear boundary between the offline world and the online world. Those who were on the move were not connected, those who were connected were immobile.

Now connection Points like telephone booths have disappeared: it seems like a geological era since people used to use tokens or plastic cards to make phone calls, but that was only a few years ago. With the mobile Internet, great historical accelerations have taken place in a relatively short time, even sweeping away those who did not take this into account. Some of our critics years ago accused us of overestimating the potential of the Net and new technologies, many of whom now no longer exist as political subjects, they have become extinct.

With the advent of the smartphone, a dualism falls away: we are constantly connected, at home, at work, on the road. For some time now, Internet use from a mobile location has surpassed access from a fixed location. And we have become transparent to the system: our every search or conversation can be recorded and transformed into data. Mobile phones are our digital prostheses, connected to the data processing centres of companies and states, so capital increasingly ‘invades’ us.
Physical and digital intertwine until they become one.

Once this intertwining has occurred, the conditions are in place for the advent of a ‘historical singularity’, beyond which, we will snap into another type of reality, in which man and machine will merge. Some accuse us of having a vision similar to that of the transhumanists, i.e. we have an uncritical view of technological ‘progress’. We do not believe it is a problem of technology but of who uses it and for what purposes.

In the Limes video mentioned at the beginning, it is said, among other things, that a new revolution is underway that empowers our brains, that extends them, freeing humanity from forced labour, that is capable of taking our eyes high into the sky, far from Earth, thanks to satellites. One is reminded of what James Lovelock said in the book ‘Gaia – New Ideas on Ecology’: the biosphere becomes self-aware when the first astronauts see the Earth from space and photograph it, sending the images back to humans on Earth. It is as if the Planet for the first time looked in the mirror and saw what it looked like.

Following Lovelock’s reasoning, we can understand the astronauts aboard the spacecraft as part of Gaia, of the planet Earth, an extension of it, as are the satellites, which produce data that we relate to each other, on which calculations are made by computers, which make it possible to make predictions that were previously impossible. Man, thanks to industry, is empowered, evolves as a species, becomes truly himself, continuing the exploration of his surroundings: land, seas, oceans and... space.

The ability to make scientifically based predictions is a prerequisite for any significant ‘reversal of praxis’, which for the current we refer to – is synonymous with social design. Technological development, the integration of production, the ‘rectification’ of the world, require a general reorganisation by a force that overturns the current social anarchy and brings with it order.

The human species is producing technologies that run counter to the current relations of production. Communist content is pressing to break free from the capitalist envelope. Therefore the political break will come as a consequence: if we were to say that chaos prevails today but that within it we can glimpse the emergence of order, it would mean that we are accepting the miracle of a kind of communist transubstantiation: instead communism is there. It is a matter of having the key. As it is written on the home page of our website, the structure of tomorrow’s society is the fuse that will blow up today’s. From the chaotic fibrillation of social atoms, new structures will arise.

Chaos represents the transition to a new social form. Theorists of self-organisation, e.g. Stuart Kauffman, describe the edge of chaos as that ‘borderland’ that makes new configurations of matter possible.

The enormous amount of data produced in recent years has led to the need for a science of data: the ability to analyse, extrapolate and relate heterogeneous data in order to discover the links between different phenomena and predict future ones. This new science is based on sophisticated statistical methods, computer science, mathematics and information theory.
Artificial’ eyes in space

Satellites observe the Earth, draw useful data from it, which are processed by supercomputers, such as the one at Leonardo in Bologna (ranked as the fourth most powerful in the world in terms of computing power). A series of two-way links runs from Earth to space and vice versa. It was realised that if one does not have the computing capacity to deal with an increasing flow of information, one can overcome the problem by linking several computers and simulating neural networks.

Today, satellites give the bourgeoisie the possibility of observing small movements on Earth, mapping territories, detecting risks, facilitating, for example, precision agriculture (optimising soil productivity by analysing the chemistry and physics of the planet, including the composition of the air).

And, of course, they are used in war, as Limes notes in an issue entitled ‘Space is for war’ (2021).[[6]] A contributor to the Italian geopolitics magazine, Marcello Spagnulo, a member of the technical table of the Interministerial Committee for Space and Aerospace Policy, in the essay Star Capitalism. How the new space race is changing the Earth, informs us that space is no longer the exclusive domain of state agencies, but that by now, private high-tech industry is also investing heavily in the race to conquer it (if one can call a leap of a few hundred kilometres in relation to galactic distances a conquest), both for the search for raw materials and to occupy the orbits around the Earth with their satellites.[[7]]

For Spagnulo, giga-companies are using satellites ‘to shape a new economic model’, and perhaps the clearest example is the Californian company SpaceX founded in 2002 by Elon Musk. Who is not the only protagonist in this story. Jeff Bezos, head of Amazon, is also investing in the design of spaceships and rockets, and so is the capitalist Richard Branson with his Virgin Galactic.
Space, Spagnulo reports, is filling up with satellites:

“Think of the fact that within this decade an inordinately larger number of satellites will be launched into orbit around our planet than all those launched in the last half-century. From 1957 to 2018, the number of objects put into orbit each year never exceeded 200, but by 2019, it has skyrocketed to 1,600 with an exponential growth that does not seem to stop.”

So the global satellite business has opened up: the US and China are the biggest global players. A Chinese company has sold satellites to Wagner, which is a private military company based in Russia. And a US company, Interorbital System based in California, has put on sale do-it-yourself kits to assemble micro-satellites.

Italy has long since given up researching and building launchers but is well present with satellite components. For example, the orbiting station Prisma (HyperSpectral Application Mission PRecursor) scans the earth’s surface, detecting its qualities and, above all, the variations between them, processing them as if the analysis laboratories with their mega-data and their memories had been transported directly into orbit.

What we live in is a (potentially) intelligent system, albeit one that has been crippled by the persistence of capitalism. We could say that the General Intellect of which Marx speaks in the Grundrisse has moved out and now includes, albeit in infinitesimal quantities, space.
Black Mirror

Today, we usually speak of smart phones, smart cards, smart cities, smart cars, etc. Any object can become smart by connecting to the Net. The other side of the coin is an increasingly stupid social system, i.e. one that uses the intelligence of things for anti-human purposes, such as growth in consumption at all costs.

When we speak of a smart city, we mean a technologically advanced urban area that uses various electronic methods to collect data about itself, process it and design interventions of an urban, architectural, environmental, energy-efficient etc. nature. In the capitalist sphere, this data also serves the purpose of control and thus has a peek-a-boo function.

A few years ago, Sidewalk Labs, a Google-affiliated company, announced that it wanted to build a smart neighbourhood in Toronto, Canada. By means of sensors scattered everywhere and the use of cutting-edge materials, the company aimed to make every single part of the urban agglomeration ‘smart’. The project attracted a lot of criticism regarding the end of privacy and totalitarian control of every single movement or activity of citizens.

China makes extensive use of technology for population control: it has installed 200 million cameras throughout the country, mainly in metropolises. Connected to artificial intelligence systems, they are trained to recognise the social temperature (likelihood of protests or riots) from citizens’ movements and the expression on their faces. The Chinese government is testing the social credit system: with the collaboration of Alibaba and Tencent, two companies that own the most popular social networks in China, it tracks and judges citizens’ behaviour by assigning rewards or penalties to their every move. This experiment is also intended to assess their conduct from a political point of view.
But all states have used digital geolocation systems to monitor citizens’ movements and contacts during and after the pandemic.

Moving from states to companies, from East to West, the e-commerce company Amazon applies a system of rewards and punishments in its warehouses based on employees’ performance, which is tracked by the scanner they use to move goods.

Black Mirror, the series promoted on Netflix, dedicated an episode to this reality, ‘Free Fall’: the protagonist lives in a dystopian reality based on the rating scores accumulated on social networks. It is easy to deduce that reality is now at the same level or even surpassing science fiction. As Fabio Chiusi writes in his book Io non sono qui (I am not here), the Black Mirror series unsettles us not so much for its glimpse into the future as for its revealing glimpse into our present.

China, we have pointed out, during the pandemic took extreme measures to block movement, made possible partly by its agrarian and urban structure, partly by technology. But the extraordinary statistical results were achieved, even more than with the use of the latter, thanks to the possibility of deporting or blocking hundreds of millions of people, the most effective brutal method of dealing with any pandemic.

Against the pervasive control, generalised worldwide, hybrid movements sprang up (no green pass) claiming the citizen’s right to privacy, chanting slogans against science and technology and in favour of ‘freedom’.[[8]]

Sociologist Shoshana Zuboff, in her essay The Capitalism of Surveillance, describes how the Web giants continuously extract data from citizens’ activities in order not only to understand their business preferences but also to target them. Web companies have developed extremely sophisticated techniques in this regard. The author mourns the death of individual freedom, of free will, of democracy, of law: in practice, of bourgeois illusions.

It is good that this veil of hypocrisy falls: we know that free will is a fiction, that we are determined, especially in this social form; that if today we are strongly conditioned by influencers, before we were no less so by our family of origin, our village or town, school, church, television, the mafias, the superstitions of past generations.

Although driven by an insatiable thirst for profit, the big tech giants are unconsciously but objectively helping to steer mankind into the future, building infrastructures that can be used for other purposes, such as combating the remnants of anti-social behaviour, which today is continually stimulated by the need to compete with one’s peers.

Reading the above essay brings to mind the famous film Matrix, in which it is shown how, on Earth, a despotic system controlled by machines has been established. These power themselves at the expense of man, who is reduced to a kind of disposable battery and made to live in a virtual reality so that he does not rebel. The cinema has indulged in this theme, with many variations (Minority Report, Elysium, Ex Machina, Transcendence, etc.), showing that the problem is felt to be topical.

According to widespread opinions, with the development of artificial intelligence, there is a risk that mankind will become the victim of a Digital Big Brother (see the aforementioned ‘social credit system’ in China). The ‘democratic’ critics of antivirus social control measures had drawn attention to the risk of ‘pandemic surveillance’ remaining even after the epidemic had passed (The Eyes of the Virus. Pandemic and Surveillance, David Lyon). Today, the same politically crushed people raise the alarm about violated human rights and argue for ‘data justice’. But revolutions do not rest on ‘opinions’.

We, belonging to a current in which we see ourselves as explorers of tomorrow,[[9]] we look beyond capitalism, and register that there is already a symbiotic relationship with a technology that is no longer antagonistic. This, which may seem like a reckless statement, should instead be interpreted as a self-fulfilling reality. In spite of the perplexities and arguments raised, what Marx stated (essays of the future are already present within this society) and Engels confirmed (Bismarck works for us) still applies.

The German essayist Alexander Pschera, who has dealt with the strange phenomenon called ‘dataism’, a new philosophy according to which the world is an uninterrupted flow of data, wrote in his book Dataism: Towards Big Data: Critique of Anonymous Morality that practically all observers agree in their criticism of the way data is collected, processed and used, but do not put forward any well-founded alternatives.

‘Our relationship with the world of data, which has absorbed the world of politics, medicine and culture, is deeply governed by fear,’ he says. ‘We are afraid that we will lose something, that we will miss something without seeing the productive gain for our society that can come from data collection and analysis. An alternative project sees the human face in big data. Formulating a fearless freedom in its ethical projection is the primary task of the new postacademic discipline of dataism.’

Of course, we are not criticising the bourgeoisie and petty-bourgeoisie for their moralistic and idealistic drift. The transition from the realm of necessity to that of freedom is not a question of ethics or morality but of the maturation of social productive forces. What matters is the anonymous movement of millions of individuals (now billions). In all the critical publications we have cited regarding the data society, there is concern about the formation of a panoptic system that everyone spies on and controls. But to attribute to humans a subjective view of the evolutionary process is to deny what we have always said about free will. Wanting to return to the ‘good’ old days when technology was less ‘invasive’ is not possible, we can only move towards another social form.
Assemblages
Geoff Mulgan in the essay Big Mind. The collective intelligence that can change the world addresses the evolution of life on Earth and the evolution of knowledge through a single key: assemblage.

In fact, just as our brain works by assembling many different elements, so does the social brain, which is the combination of humans, machines and networks. Nowadays, it is difficult to think of a biological intelligence that is not in some way connected to the technological one. Our species has evolved through a multi-millennial feedback with the tool, achieving a symbiotic relationship with it. As things stand today, it is no longer just a matter of giving humans energy, strength and functionality through prostheses, but a transition is being made from a relationship between two separate subjects to a fusion into one. As in the case of the experiments by Neuralink (a neurotechnology company founded by Musk), in which a chip for human-machine communication was inserted into a human brain.

The Internet is the result of the assembly of brains and computers, which in turn are assemblies of neurons and microchips. The Net is one of the clearest manifestations of the social brain. In the present state of affairs, the order embedded in the immense collection of information that is continuously being processed takes the form of an increasing capacity for self-reproduction. For instance, the realisation of a programme like Google Maps required the assembly of different technologies put in relation to each other, and at this point residing in memories that are ultimately non-places (servers, satellites, local networks, etc.).

The next step for Google Maps was to develop an API to be able to install the service in other sites. It was created by a start-up capable of providing images and data to drivers and vice versa. Anyone, therefore, can contribute to the development of the service.

The Net leads us to think in ways that are apparently new but in reality as old as our species. On the Net, for example, we grasp the importance of connections, we see the world as a set of relationships as humanity saw it at the dawn of its evolution. Therefore, what makes the difference is not so much the building of structures from scratch but the connecting of those that already exist:

‘Many experiments have studied how large groups manage to solve complex problems with the help of intelligent machines. The open source movement has shown that large-scale collaboration can be practical, efficient and dynamic and has provided much of the software for the internet. Its ethos is based on parsimony – programming ‘with the laziness of a fox’, according to the formula of Linus Torvalds, one of its pioneers – but the cumulative outcome is extraordinary. Others have used computers to manage people, for instance by creating ‘flash teams’ of problem solvers, breaking work down into modular elements and then managing their sequential reassembly. Some of the most interesting hybrid assemblies use platforms to aggregate and orchestrate genius on an ever-increasing scale.’ (Big Mind, Geoff Mulgan)
And its all being done for free.

We can think of our world as one big assemblage. There are still barriers, represented by corporate and national boundaries, that prevent its progress towards a single world production plan, but the current social form will not be able to block this process for much longer. Communism is a material force, it can be slowed down, hindered, but it cannot be stopped. Marx and Engels, as we have recalled, said that ‘if we could not already discern, hidden in this society – as it is – the material conditions of production and relations between men, corresponding to a classless society, every effort to blow it up would be quixotic’, as we repeat without pause.

Mulgan’s book describes the formation of a collective intelligence emerging from the combination of humans and machines. On a global level, even the bourgeoisie are beginning to see how a wide range of resources – from satellite networks to university laboratories, from public health officials to teachers – could co-ordinate and form something akin to a single social brain; or, to use another image that has relevance to the biological world, a global nervous system.

Methods such as the ‘digital twin’ are possible because previous assemblages have in turn made new ones possible. This self-similar structure is reminiscent, on a different scale, of that described by the Hungarian philosopher Arthur Koestler, who coined the term holon to define a complex system composed of other subsystems, which are themselves holons. A holonic organisation is thus a ‘self-organising structure’. Given the ‘rectification’ of the world, it is impossible to analyse one component in isolation, everything is linked in two directions. What is needed is precisely a theory of networks, a systemic approach to understanding social becoming.
But what is the digital twin practically?
To create a ‘digital twin’ you need:
1) physical products in real space;
2) virtual products in virtual space;
3) systems for linking and exchanging information between the two planes.

It should be made clear that it must be possible for the digital model to interact with the physical one through direct action on systems, infrastructures or other, through the coordination of machines or humans, or through a combination of the two.

It should be clear by now that data are the most important elements to make the appearance of the ‘digital twin’ possible: they are the trait d’union between physical and digital. The origins of the idea are to be found in the essay Mirror Worlds (1991) by the computer scientist David Gelernter, but the concept of the ‘digital twin’ was introduced at the beginning of the 21st century by Michael Grieves, an expert in industrial engineering, who described it during a university course as the virtual copy of a physical object.

According to the vision of two philosophers who have dealt with the subject, Maria Pia Rossignaud and Derrick De Kerckhove, the ‘digital twin’ is ‘an avatar, it is our life told by data. It signifies the two-way universal access between man and the network’ (Beyond Orwell. The digital twin).

The ‘digital twin’ originated in industry for the design of machines or parts of them with the idea of remotely monitoring their use. It receives real-time data from the physical world and uses it to modify the digital one; in this way, it can come up with simulations and predictions. The most interesting aspect of the ‘digital twin’ is its ability to influence the simulation on which it acts; it is no longer disconnected from its physical reference object or system. The system is based on feedback (two-way flow) between the virtual and physical components. There are ‘digital twins’ of components or parts, systems and processes.[[10]]

A process ‘digital twin’ is one that simulates the operation of a production plan, i.e. a dynamic set of parts and systems. Of a physical factory, a virtual copy exists within a computer system. The ‘digital twin’ is constantly updated by its physical duplicate and vice versa. The significant aspect is the ability to transform data into something measurable. Remember that science is based on measurement and thus on numbers.

Digital simulation models of any object can be created, models that change when their physical counterparts change. The first area of use of the forerunner of a ‘digital twin’ is that of NASA as described in the film Apollo 13 (Ron Howard): on 13 April 1970, three astronauts who were in a spacecraft bound for the moon reported that an oxygen tank had ruptured, disabling some of the systems, and sent a message that later became famous: ‘Houston, we have a problem’. To help them return to Earth, NASA’s mission control centre used the command module simulators on which the crew had been trained to work out new manoeuvring procedures. The simulators were largely physical models, as computers at the time were less powerful than those of today. But it was possible to use the data transmitted from the damaged spacecraft to recreate the problems and thus understand how to solve them. The Apollo 13 mission was described by insiders as ‘NASA’s most successful failure’.

Today, there is no longer a need for physical models, computerised ones, which can be modified with respect to the changing physical reality, are more functional. The ‘digital twin’, as well as being used for the design of objects, can represent the state or position of physical objects or systems in real time.

Digital twins’ in industry developed in the wake of the automation of production processes and the spread of Internet connections. General Electric was one of the first companies to produce a bit model of Boeing aircraft turbines. This made it possible to constantly monitor the object remotely. Detecting problems before they occur is functional both in terms of safety and economic costs. It makes maintenance a targeted operation. When the turbine is sold, a bit model of it is associated with it. The physical turbine has sensors located at particular points that continuously transmit data to some control room where the digital turbine is located.

As The Economist writes, ‘digital twins’ constantly monitor the status of airliners, replicating Amazon’s vast supply chain so that the company can accurately predict sales volume months or even years in advance.[[11]] In the case of Uber, when the user requests a ride via the app, he becomes, together with the driver and the car, part of the company’s ‘digital twin’.[[12]]

The ‘digital twin’, as we have seen, would not be possible without an enormous amount of sensors (a Formula 1 racing car can have more than 250 sensors updating its ‘digital twin’ during a grand prix[[13]]). With this technology, based on the current state of the physical object, and given the processing speed of computers, scenarios can be outlined and prompt action taken to avoid damage or accidents.

Artificial intelligence assists in all phases of the project including the simulation of the future state of an object or system, making it much easier for all types of companies to generate computer replicas and/or supervise them at a scale and speed that individuals or groups of engineers could never achieve. The ‘digital twin’ is not simply a simulator that sits alongside the physical copy: it detects malfunctions or anomalies, processes signals and sends inputs to control centres. It is not simply a modification of previous methods: ‘digital twins’ are revolutionising the way a factory is run. This is no longer a unit separate from its surroundings: with access to data from suppliers and customers, the corporate twin of the production process helps engineers to optimise flows and thus avoid bottlenecks.
From virtual Singapore to virtual capitalism
The technology of the ‘digital twin’ can also be applied to city planning.

A metropolis can be virtually reconstructed through geological, spatial and climatic statistical data and images. Singapore is the most connected city in the world and has built itself a ‘digital twin’ that architects and town planners can access to design infrastructures and see their future effects: predictions can be made based, for example, on traffic growth.

In Europe, Zurich is among the cities that have developed an advanced ‘urban digital twin’.[[14]] A ‘digital twin’ of the Earth is being developed, a project of the European Commission, Destination Earth (DestinE), a virtual, interactive replica of the Planet to enable the identification of general and regional trends, and to simulate and predict the interaction between natural phenomena and human activities. With a virtual twin of the Planet, forecasts can be updated continuously. And Destination Earth is in fact constantly correcting itself, as happens in computerised wargames. Such models obviously work as long as they are applied to a capitalist reality, because this is what they produce. To have ‘twinning’ in the absence of capital investment, one must turn to another type of society.

In fact, any virtual twin realised in the capitalist sphere detects and processes capitalist configurations and applications. In order to have a glimpse of the future, it cannot ignore, for instance, a planning of access to credit guaranteed by the banking system, guaranteed in turn by the state. It is precisely from this that capitalism in its current supreme phase needs to emerge. The example of Singapore, a city-state with a planned, and thus socialised, economy, lends itself well to illustrate the model, so much so that bourgeois economists call its permanent twin (joking but not too much) ‘Nazism with a human face’.

The cybernetic twin of today’s society offering a glimpse into the future suggests compulsory behaviour; but let us make it clear that these are internal investigations of a precise system that can only provide answers through its language and implementation possibilities. Within this scheme it is certainly possible to achieve a high level of realism even with the correction of the predetermined course. We have verified this with the analysis of MIT’s Mondo3, realised with a world model, i.e. with a ‘digital twin’ of the planet projected into the future. Mondo3 showed that capitalism was racing towards its own catastrophe and suggested the conditions to be adopted to get back on course. This was true for the compilers of the programme and for us: catastrophe was indeed on the horizon. For the majority of the bourgeoisie, however, the course was modifiable and Mondo3 received hostile criticism in its own milieu. Whereas for us, the programme showed with sufficient accuracy the end that capitalism would come to. In one and the same dynamic system, two opposite contents could be read: for us and the bourgeoisie disaster on the one hand, and on the other only salvation with course corrections. But these were practically impossible for the bourgeoisie to achieve (e.g. they could never have eliminated the credit system, nor dissipation, nor the lack of coordination necessary to influence reality) in the absence of an unimaginable world government whose executive could take measures capable of changing the capitalist dynamic at work.

Today, as then, the virtual model of capitalism implemented by the data coming from the various bourgeois research centres would prove to those who programmed it that its game over for the system. Such a model would certainly have a catastrophic trend, and might give hints as to how to delay the crash (‘causes antagonistic to the fall in the profit rate’). But it could give rise to doubts within the bourgeoisie, among its shrewdest technicians. The crisis of senile capitalism will increase ideological and practical capitulations in the face of ‘Marxism’ and with it the phenomenon of class transfusions.
The capitalist system, as complex as it is, functions according to simple rules such as the triad ‘take’, ‘process’ and ‘input’ information.

Input certain data into computers, deterministically ‘output’ results. The output consists of diagrams that speak for themselves: the concentration of wealth at one pole and poverty at the other is not sustainable for long, all attempts to reform the system have been exhausted (social democracy, fascism, demofascism). Among the most realistic hypotheses, the programme points to the outbreak of a revolution.
Oxfam, an international confederation of non-profit organisations, publishes an annual report on inequality. The one for 2024 focuses on the fact that political power serves the few:

‘High and growing inequality is a sadly distinctive feature of the age in which we live. Recent severe crises have widened social inequalities and rifts, ushering in what we have no hesitation in describing as the ‘decade of great divides’ with billions of people forced to see their frailties grow and bear the brunt of epidemics, caravansions, conflicts, increasingly frequent extreme weather events, and a handful of super-rich multiplying their fortunes at paroxysmal rates.’
But this is capitalism, there isn’t anything else.
Cyber-security

Data is the new capital. The companies (such as Facebook, Google, Amazon, Apple, etc.) that collect and process it have enormous power to control society, and in some cases have a stock market value that exceeds the GDP of states.

Both companies and states must continually step up research and development of technologies to secure their data. They must avoid attacks by hackers, who damage or steal them, and for this they increase the cyber-security sector, aimed at detecting attacks and responding immediately to cyber incursions. To do this, automatisms are needed; the time humans have to choose may be too long to foil a cyber threat.

Think of drones: we already see self-coordinating swarms in action today. They will be increasingly deployed in both civil and military environments and will require adequate defences. Humans find it hard to monitor and understand their own movements, so we need an automatic defence system that responds quickly to threats.

In an interview in Arlington last year, Washington’s Deputy Secretary of Defence Kathleen Hicks said that given China’s technological advances, we need to accelerate research into ‘swarming’, both in the strategic and tactical domains:

‘Imagine self-propelled floating or flying systems, powered by the sun and other virtually unlimited resources, full of sensors in abundance, enough to provide us with new and reliable sources of information in near real time. Fleets of ground-based systems that provide new logistical support, conduct reconnaissance to keep troops safe, or protect Department of Defence infrastructure. Constellations of systems in orbit, launched into space dozens at a time, in such numbers that it is impossible to neutralise them all. Flocks of systems flying at all kinds of altitudes and performing a variety of missions, based on what we saw in Ukraine. They could be deployed from larger aircraft, launched by land or sea troops, or take off on their own’.[[15]]

The war of the future, now in gestation, will be one of algorithms against algorithms, autonomous machines against autonomous machines. Enlistment campaigns aim not only to increase the infantry, but to equip armies with hackers, computer technicians, engineers, capable of handling sophisticated tools. In the article ‘Wargame’ (n+1 no. 50, 2021) we wrote:

‘The British Armed Forces Staff is convinced that playing wargames is useful to the nation because it accustoms citizens to thinking in terms of conflict and competition even for fields other than war. It is not just any model, he says, but a programme for thinking. This, with some modifications, would be in line with what we also say: in the wargame man experiences a situation, the programme calculates it. The programme is not to be confused with constructivist simulation, the creation of artificial models of reality. Nor with a set of simple partial functions which, when assembled, lead to complex results. A simulation, however perfect, is not a wargame but only its engine, while the data that informs it are its fuel.’

As well as in the civil sphere, ‘digital twin’ models are used extensively in the military sphere. We have to imagine them as organisms, both physical and virtual, that learn to defend themselves against a pathogen, such as a computer virus, and that evolve and anticipate the enemy’s threats.

In the civil as in the military sphere, we are crossing the boundary between the biological and technological worlds, as demonstrated for instance by the swarms of self-organised drones we have talked about.

Our society has become biotechnological, perhaps it has been since man first chipped the first stone to make it a useful tool, starting a process that has led to the creation of a digital copy of itself, a virtual duplicate that co-designs the future with and for ‘us’. As Marshall McLuhan says: ‘We create our tools, which then in turn transform us’ (The Tools of Communication). Giuseppe O. Longo wrote as early as 2001 in Homo technologicus:

‘So important is technology, that it contributes to forming the cognitive (and active) categories of man, conditioning his development. The distinction between man and technology is not as clear-cut as is sometimes claimed, because technology contributes to forming the essence of man, and furthermore, the evolution of technology has become the evolution of man. If today biological evolution is at a standstill, cultural evolution is faster than ever: but the separation between the two is artificial, since the two processes have now become intertwined in a ‘biocultural’ or ‘biotechnological’ evolution’.

Hacker attacks can cause enormous damage to a state’s strategic infrastructure (power grids, transport systems, banks, hospitals, government sites), an example being the attack by allegedly Iranian ‘hackers’ on Albania in 2022, which had blocked its national IT infrastructure for weeks. Hackers could directly target the ‘digital twin’ of an individual, a group or a company by appropriating sensitive data and using them for various purposes.

States with advanced technological means have already started a new kind of war. Significant is the (unclaimed) attack by Israel in Lebanon on pagers and walkie-talkies belonging to members of the Hezbollah network.

Digital twins of security systems are produced. A cyber-security system can generate a ‘digital twin’ of itself on which to simulate attacks and test how the system reacts. One can detect flaws and try to remedy them in advance. One can compile a ‘digital twin’ of a software and subject it to stress tests.

All in all, these are methods and objectives common to all companies in this world to supply all kinds of products, but the revolution that Marx talks about, and we with him, lies in the substantial difference between those that base their existence on the numerical twin (project) and the others. The factory is continually self-reproducing in the permanent repair shop, now computerised and automated.

From the Internet portal Defence Online[[16]], we learn, for example, that in the military sector, which is more delicate and complex than others, cyber simulations are congruent with extremely differentiated objectives within a single system, where there is a single command line (technological and political pyramid hierarchy) and a single network transmission of information (sending and receiving data via hubs). The advanced integration of functions was well identified by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in his end-of-term speech (17 January 1961), regarding the danger posed by the ‘military-industrial complex’.

The network of companies working in the field of cyber-security now pervades the entire society. From the Lab level, where new methods and technologies are developed, personnel are recruited directly at universities, laboratories are connected with each other and with other research centres. Public and private entities network, different skills are brought together, and what emerges is something that is more than the sum of the parts.

Today’s society, in order to defend itself, is forced to restructure in order to keep up with the challenges of the future. Capitalism adopts a networked functioning in its state-of-the-art production structures. As written in the Communist Party Manifesto, bourgeois society cannot exist without continuously revolutionising the instruments of production, the relations of production and thus all social relations. Capitalism has developed to such an extent that it is forced to deny itself at an ever higher level. As a totally inhuman and therefore disorganic form, it perceives that in order to delay its end it must try to homeostatise itself, and it does so by copying the workings of nature at best.
Biomimicry is that set of technologies that imitate the functioning of nature, drawing inspiration from it to solve problems in human society.

We could say that the ‘Italian’ Communist Left in presenting the Theses on the Tactics of the Communist Party of Italy (Rome, 1922) had made an operation of biomimicry ahead of historical times by contrasting democratic centralism (conquest of the majority of the proletariat, discretisation) with organic centralism (everything is in relation, continuity). It was not a matter of devising a particular form of organisation, but of ‘copying’ nature’s way of functioning.

Today, the bourgeoisie is realising that working with networks requires a new kind of paradigm. Some academic studies on self-organisation focus on the need for humanity to organise itself without top-down structures but by imitating the ‘reticular’ functioning of nature: distributed information, units acting autonomously but integrated, a kind of ‘organic centralism’ applied to companies, schools and armies. The problem is that the structures of this society are hierarchical, being the product of the social division of labour, and if they have to adapt to a situation that is too different from their origins, they tend to disintegrate.

If the counter-revolution is active, it means that the revolution is on the march and capitalism is forced to work for ‘us’, even if this today means maximum exploitation (extraction of relative surplus value) of labour power through technology. Dominance of dead labour over living labour.
A digital twin of ourselves

With the current state of knowledge, it is possible to reproduce the characteristics of a human being by copying his genetic make-up, processing the information produced when he surfs the Net (the Web knows more about us than our friends![[17]]), by monitoring body functions through various devices (e.g. ‘smart’ wrist sensors).

By exploring sites, shopping online, putting likes on social networks, in short, by living, we sow the world with all the information needed to draw up our profile, i.e. we leave a diffuse digital footprint, which can be compartmentalised into specific subsets.

Just as the human body can be monitored with various types of more or less intelligent, centralised sensors, so too can the environment in which we live be monitored in order to reproduce models next to the real system that bear a high resemblance to the originals.

There are those who worry, even in Marxist circles, about the loss of privacy that the spread of such systems would entail for the use of data for profit. But it is not simply a question of systemised espionage. What is happening is much more complex and concerns the advancement in this society of a hitherto little considered collective intelligence of a type we have already discussed: ‘swarming’. In addition to the now customary collective intelligence of machine systems that imitate human skills with great accuracy, there are systems that imitate biological intelligence with increasing accuracy.

Humanity has reached the point where a bifurcation occurs: on the one hand, systems that develop by autopoiesis (i.e., that sustain and reproduce themselves using their own internal elements and qualities), on the other hand, those that develop by design. The advent of evolutionary development based on only one of the two branches of the bifurcation leads to conflict between them. If mankind is to overcome the conflict between the Bee and the Architect, i.e. between two powerful forces of evolution, it will have to become aware of the fact that only symbiosis between them can guarantee a society based on the reversal of praxis, i.e. harmonious development through the increasing importance of planned existence over spontaneous existence.
From the Communist Party Manifesto onwards, we know that the proletariat has nothing to lose but its chains, it has a world to gain, to design, a world where there will be no ownership of any kind.

The ideological short-circuit that is generated within the bourgeois class (in what are its ideological cornerstones), which understands private property as an inalienable right of the individual, but then is unable to guarantee it since cases of dossiers and mass espionage punctually break out is interesting. Today, it is difficult, if not impossible, to be the ‘owner’ of all the data we generate, as shown, for example, by the Cambridge Analytica case, a company that used the data of millions of Facebook users for the election campaign in favour of Donald Trump.

Marshall McLuhan said that fighting for privacy in the age of electricity is like fighting against a tsunami. He is echoed by Mark Zuckerberg who says that today privacy is practically finished as a social norm.

Not all bourgeoisie, however, see the non-privatist era that is opening up as a bad thing. Jeremy Rifkin, for example, addresses this issue in his essay The Zero Marginal Cost Society, going against the mainstream thinking:

‘Connecting everyone and everything in a global neural network means moving humanity out of the age of privacy, the hallmark of the modern era, and into the age of transparency. Although it has long been considered a fundamental right, privacy has never been an innate right. Indeed, throughout human history, until the modern era, life was lived more or less publicly, as befits the most social species on earth.’

Private property is denied by capitalist development itself, which is dispossessing the small and middle class in favour of the large economic concentrations, the large financial monopolies. The two biggest investment funds, BlackRock and Vanguard, manage about 1/5 of the world’s wealth. They have cross-shareholdings between them, which is why it is unclear where the ownership of one begins and ends. These financial agglomerations control the world’s largest companies, banks and public infrastructure. Amazon is bidding to become humanity’s only emporium, Facebook runs a social network that connects three billion people, Google aims to be the most used search engine.
Capital is virtualising with the digitalisation of everything, we are therefore entering the era of transparency, everything we do when we are connected is recorded.

If the described technologies are now functional for social control and targeted advertising, it cannot be denied that being equipped with a ‘digital twin’ could give each of us greater individual and collective potential. The tendency is to gather all the data about us in a single platform on the cloud.

These copies of ourselves could help us design, plan and decide. Think of Google Maps that helps us get to our destination by finding the best road route, the one with the least traffic. If there is an accident, the navigator suggests an alternative route to the one initially chosen. There and then, when we are driving the car, we do not think that Google Maps is denying our free will, yet a not insignificant part in our ‘choices’ to travel by car or public transport is decided by a technological system connected to other systems.

“We manufacture these calculators, but in return they build us. There are no longer many everyday gestures – shopping, travelling, personal or professional decisions – that are not guided by an infrastructure of calculations. When this suddenly fails, as when a fault interrupts telephone traffic, we are lost.” (What Algorithms Dream of, Dominique Cardon)

Without a mobile phone we feel incomplete because it is as if we lost an eye or a limb, these technologies are now part of ourselves, they are a development of the ancestral tool with which we have evolved over the millennia. Perhaps tomorrow while we sleep or rest we will have a ‘digital twin’ working for us, or the species will decide that such a presence of technology will no longer be useful. What is important is that since there is no longer private property, not even of one’s own body, society will think in terms of satisfying the needs of the species.
A digital copy of planet Earth

The neo-Luddite critics of the new technologies say that we are facing a system that, if we cannot control it, will control us. This is true: but the problem – let us repeat it – is not the technology, but those who have a monopoly on it.

Dead labour dominates over living labour, but dead labour is the one produced by our species. On the cover of issue 54 of this magazine we have shown an image representing Minkowski’s spacetime, in which one can see a symmetry between past and future. In such a model, the lower part of the ‘cone of light’, the past, contains all the configurations of events that prepared the upper part, just as the future contains the past that determined it. The ‘cone of light’ lends itself to some reflections on the role of the machine, which can be a factor of exploitation (capitalism) or liberation (communism) depending on the point of observation.

We place ourselves in n+1, it is from this vantage point that we look at the current social form, n. On the other hand, to understand a system one must look from the perspective of a higher order system. As noted in Trajectory and Catastrophe,[[18]] in Marx’s Grundrisse we read the novel of objectivised labour:

“In this Transformation [due to automation] the pillar of Production and Wealth is neither the immediate Labour performed by Man, nor the Labour Time employed, but the Appropriation of his own general Productive Force, his Intelligence of Nature and his Dominion over it by virtue of his existence as a Social Body – in a word, the development of the Social Individual”.

Bourgeois society no longer has a future, it cannot overcome n, i.e. itself. Capitalism has developed to the point of producing technologies that mimic the functioning of the brain; hence, self-learning machines that copy biological mechanisms.

Technology is pervading us, which means we are (potentially) reuniting with ourselves, with our human-industry being. As capitalism persists, however, this transition becomes very delicate and even dangerous, because it is profit and not our well-being that is at stake. We are the ‘naked monkey’ Desmond Morris talks about, handling the nuclear bomb without being aware of it. It is worrying that these technologies are in the hands of the bourgeoisie, a class that is groping in the dark and does not know the society it has helped to build. A sentence by Bordiga during a meeting in Bologna on 13 November 1960, reported in issue 15-16 of our magazine, is significant:
‘We cannot leave such power and such ignorance in the hands of the bourgeoisie at the same time, the future of the species depends on it.’

Returning to the ‘digital twins’, as we have seen, they also serve to test the products a company intends to make. The relationship between producer and consumer is being transformed. This dualism is also breaking down. The term prosumer was coined by Alvin Toffler in his book The Third Wave: the individual becomes both consumer and producer of goods. Once, the relationship between seller and consumer ended with the sale of the goods. Now there is a continuous link between producer, seller and consumer, not least because some goods have become ‘intelligent’ and require continuous maintenance. The user provides data to the producer that allows the latter to adapt the product to the demands.
Think of the mobile phone or computer and the continuous updates that are made to operating systems. Connection that serves both the user and the company.

The future society is that of the continuous (unpublished Chapter VI of Capital: Continuous Goods). It is being formed within this by breaking down existing dualisms. We can compare the Web to realised communism: the characteristic of the Web is to connect everything, to break down barriers.

Atoms are being duplicated in bits. The advantage is that in the virtual world one can go back, in the physical world one cannot, at least on a macroscopic level. The bridge built of concrete or iron is a finished work, the virtual bridge can be built billions of times over, and each time better than the last. One jumps into the virtual world to solve problems in the physical one. Those involved in the virtual replica of the Earth project claim that the biggest problem is to connect all existing data: from the planet’s temperature to weather forecasts, from energy to transport.[[19]] It is a matter of connecting satellites, data centres, tracking stations on land and at sea. Connecting all these sensors will take time, but the problem is not so much technical, it is political. A single global body would be needed to achieve this.
By constantly using social networks we are already projected into the ‘metaverse’, and the ‘digital twin’ is a virtual extension of ourselves:

‘Because of its characteristics and the opportunity to be concretely experienced, the Metaverse is not just a model of the physical universe, it is instead its ‘digital twin’. We are dealing with a space of interaction that converges and involves the physical dimension, however understood, and the virtual dimension together: to speak of twins means that we are not dealing with a mere representation or simulation, but with a two-way flow of data that generates a close interconnection between the two dimensions. The exchange of information does not only concern the actuality, what happens here and now, but also elaborates possible scenarios, so that it is possible to reason in a predictive mode, tackling problems before they occur and assessing in advance what might happen as a result of the choices made and decisions taken’. (Metaverse and digital twins. The new alliance between natural and artificial networks, Silvano Tagliagambe)
Tools to unite physical and digital

In the field of so-called augmented reality, the necessary equipment makes it possible for the user to range through different scenarios that can vary at will according to his or her preferred agenda. This field has not been very successful on the market, but makes the possibilities of a close interrelation between physical and virtual obvious. Wearing dedicated equipment (goggles, gloves, suits, microphones, etc.), using voice commands or movements it is possible to play music, send messages and film what one sees. Thanks to ‘generative’ artificial intelligence, computers (wearable or otherwise) are ‘learning’ to listen, read, watch and recognise recurring conformations.[[20]]

The specialised technical tools, hardware and software, that underpin what appears to be a commodity sector like any other, have so far been used mainly by gamers, but the features of computerised gaming are making them commonplace.

This is a further step towards an integrated cyber-physical system. On closer inspection, the integration between programmes, machines and procedures is galloping and gathering ever larger subsets, made up of parts that are increasingly similar in modelling and use for purposes that are related to the ‘digital twin’ we are dealing with here. The Pentagon’s ‘Middle East’ wargame model increasingly resembles the ‘Middle East’ wargame model of the wargame enthusiast (and vice versa). If the game and its purposes described in the design and rulebook are sufficiently detailed, and the power of the machines used is compatible with the details, the two reality twins, one residing in Washington and the other at the player’s home, are not dissimilar (Norbert Wiener, the father of cybernetics, said that the best model of a cat is another cat. If we adopt the same tolerance criterion for the moves allowed to the two players, we will have the other cat considered in Wiener’s example). By working on the differences to optimise the two models we will obtain, at the limit, two twin systems. It has already happened in reality: when the US attacked Iraq in the First Gulf War, it received and accepted a proposal for collaboration from a private company that produced wargames.[[21]]

Other examples can be given about the ‘digital twin’. ENI in its 3D training centre in San Donato Milanese provides personnel working in the group’s plants with virtual reality visors and a sensorised glove that allows them to operate in the ‘digital twin’ of one of its plants by simulating interventions of various kinds. The same thing can be done in other areas: factories, armies, hospitals.

There have already been attempts at cyber-physical control of industrial production in the past, but these were very rudimentary experiments compared to the means available today. We are talking about the Cybersyn project in Chile in the early 1970s developed by Stafford Beer, an attempt to cybernetically operate a country’s industry through data that was collected and then sorted in a command room. This was made possible by feedback between the centre and the periphery.

Something similar, quite spontaneously, FIAT had done, as we wrote in the article ‘Imagine a factory...’ (n+1, no. 2). Instead of the old top-down structure, it became a set of production cells integrated into the overall system that seemed to have no boundaries: industry became a system of sensor-actuators, a network of relations similar to that of a biological organism. Today, logistics is an assembly line that has come out of the factory; the world is a whole network, one big factory. The ‘digital twin’ of a department could be incorporated into that of the entire factory, which in turn could be incorporated into that of an industrial district, and so on, adopting a fractal architecture to the industrial process. It is only a matter of time and it will come to that, most probably not in the current social form.
However, capitalist industry is adapting to a networked structure and the automation of production processes, and has come to duplicate itself in the virtual world.

Theoretically, there could exist a single ‘digital twin’ of the entire world industry capable of processing data coming from society and able not only to be reactive but also predictive, that is, to predict future behaviour, to make suggestions to society to avoid problems before they arise.
The algorithms that have been generated suggest how to intervene.
A digital twin of the species party

Noting that the future acts on the present, as we have reported on the site’s home page, and explored in more detail in a specific work on anti-entropy (n+1, no. 54), we might ask whether a ‘digital twin’ of the party of species, a ‘digital twin’ of the revolutionary organism suggesting to the real one the choices to be made, will be necessary tomorrow.

The question would be ill-posed, however, for the simple fact that there will not exist two parties, one physical and one digital, but a single party with multiple tools to know itself and the reality around it, and to act accordingly.

We are sure that most of the ‘communists’ in circulation today would be horrified at the idea of a digital duplicate of us dictating the line to be taken, but in reality in everyday life they are constantly assisted by technology. It is not that man becomes powerless in the face of the machine, it is that the means he has generated have become so powerful that they have become tools he cannot do without.
Today’s society is already a cyborg, as the philosopher Andy Clark (Natural-Born Cyborgs) says, and the party of the revolution will have all aspects of it in mind.

Our current has written on several occasions that we must think of today’s party-community in relation to the tasks it will have to perform in future society. In ‘Party and Class Action’ (1921) Amadeo Bordiga writes:

‘In order to give a precise, and let us say almost tangible, idea of the ‘technical’ necessity of the party, it would perhaps be advisable, if the exposition were to take an illogical aspect, to consider first the work to be done by the proletariat after coming to power, after wresting from the bourgeoisie the direction of the social machine.’

The communist party will use the incoming data from society to organise the forces of anti-form, and, having overcome the class division of society, prepare life plans for the species. Input, processing, output. The Covid-19 pandemic has shown that the world is interconnected but that coordinated action between states is not possible today. Everyone pursues their own interests: mors tua vita mea.

We have seen for ourselves that to seriously tackle a pandemic would require a one-world government, an organism ‘which carries out the defence of the human species against the dangers of physical nature and its evolutionary and probably catastrophic processes’ (‘Thesis of Naples’, 1965)

Since the immediate revolutionary programme (Forli Points, 1952) no longer admits of mediation, the revolutionary party, or whatever this structure will be called tomorrow, will necessarily have to take on problems of a social nature that the typical structures of the present society are unable to solve.

If capitalism loses power, and with it the states, which in some cases have already collapsed, some other organism will fill the void that has been created, getting rid of what is not needed and is indeed an obstacle (democracy, parliamentarianism, nationalism, etc.) to the advent of the future society.
